newsitem.title: JAPAN: No military action yet against Iraq, Japan says.
newsitem.headline: No military action yet against Iraq, Japan says.

text.p: Japan, a major ally of the United States, said on Tuesday that no military action had yet been taken against Iraq for its incursion against Kurds in the northern part of the country.
Commenting on a CNN report that U.S. B-52 bombers carrying cruise missiles had taken off from Guam, Japan's top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told his regular daily news conference:
"Japan understands that no military action has been taken (against Iraq) as of yet."
The CNN report, citing a Pentagon source, said it was not known if the bombers were heading for Iraq.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry, speaking to reporters as President Bill Clinton campaigned in Wisconsin, also had no information if the flights were connected to the Iraqi crisis.

The White House believes Iraqi President Saddam Hussein sent three tank divisions composed of 30,000 to 40,000 elite Republican Guard troops into northern Iraq to help a Kurdish faction involved in a bloody power struggle with another Kurdish group with links to Iran.
McCurry said there was evidence that some of the Iraqi forces that overran the Kurdish stronghold of Arbil over the weekend were "penetrating deeper" into northern Iraq.
The White House says U.N. Security Council resolutions approved after the 1991 Gulf War provide a legal basis for responding to Saddam's actions.
"Our interest is in keeping Saddam Hussein from believing that unjustifiable behaviour of this nature is cost-free," McCurry said.

Kajiyama said Japan, which follows developments in the Gulf closely because of its reliance on oil from the area, backed any action that would ensure Iraq followed the United Nations Security Council resolutions that ended the 1991 Gulf War.
"Japan understands U.S. military action if it is taken for the purpose of making sure Iraq follows United Nations Security Council resolutions," he said.
Officials at the Japanese Foreign Ministry said a senior U.S. diplomat visited the ministry on Tuesday morning to brief Japanese authorities on the crisis.

Meanwhile, a spokesman for the U.S. military in Japan, where about half of the 100,000 American forces in Asia are based as well as the aircraft carrier Independence and squadrons of advanced jets, said there had been no change in their operations.
"As far as I know there's no change of anything yet. None of our people have been placed on alert and there are no changes scheduled," Jon Nylander, spokesman for the U.S. Navy, told Reuters.

Nylander also said there had been no directives from the Pentagon similar to those issued in the leadup to the Gulf War, when the aircraft carrier Midway and other ships were mobilised from their bases in Japan.
